summary: Describes SOIF, the Summary Object Interchange Format, as an index object type for the Common Indexing Protocol. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to write short summary cards describing documents, so they can be shared between search systems.

questions: how do you describe web resources in soif
how does soif enable query referral
what is a soif template type
subtitle: Machine-readable summaries of web resources shared in an index mesh.

tldr.problem: Searching web resources is inefficient because keyword searches must be sent to every server in a mesh. If searches could be limited to specific attributes, query referral would work better.
tldr.mechanism: SOIF provides a machine-readable format for summary objects (metadata about web resources), each with a template type, a URL, and attribute-value pairs. These summaries can be exchanged between index servers in a mesh to guide searches.
tldr.outcome: Experimental. Query referral becomes practical for attribute-based searches, though SOIF itself received limited adoption as web searching evolved.

facts.label: Components per object
facts.value: Template type, URL, zero or more attribute-value pairs

facts.label: Encoding
facts.value: Base64 unless template type specifies otherwise

today: RFC 2655 is Experimental and has not been updated or obsoleted. SOIF as a protocol saw limited adoption in practice; web search evolved toward centralized approaches rather than mesh-based query referral.

sections.title: The Problem with Query Referral
sections.content:
RFC 2655 defines SOIF (Summary Object Interchange Format) as a way to describe web resources using structured metadata. The context is the Common Indexing Protocol (CIP), which lets index servers in a mesh guide searches toward the right servers instead of broadcasting queries everywhere.

Keyword-based free-text searches are ineffective for query referral because they match almost everything; the query must still reach every server. However, if a search specifies an attribute (such as author or title), SOIF summaries let the mesh route the query to only the servers likely to have matching resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Searching the whole internet for a keyword is like asking every bookstore to check every book. But if you search for books by a specific author, bookstores can use index cards to tell you which ones to visit.

sections.title: SOIF Structure
sections.content:
A SOIF object has three components: a template type, a URL, and zero or more attribute-value pairs. The template type identifies which attributes the object contains (for example, FILE or DOCUMENT). The URL points to the resource being described. Each attribute-value pair is tagged with a name (like Title or Author) and a size field indicating how many octets the value occupies.

Because values may contain arbitrary data, SOIF objects should be Base64-encoded unless the template type guarantees that values contain only text. When a resource has multiple authors, the naming convention Author-1, Author-2, Author-3 represents multiple values for a single attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: A SOIF card says what kind of thing it describes, where it lives, and facts about it. If there are multiple facts of the same kind (like three authors), you number them.

sections.title: Template Types and Registration
sections.content:
A template type defines the set of possible attributes for a resource class. Unregistered template types are informal and may vary by implementation; registered template types are formally specified, with defined mandatory and optional attributes, data types and encodings. The RFC notes that FILE is the most common unregistered type, used by the Harvest system, while DOCUMENT and OBJECT are other generic types.

SOIF does not define the templates themselves; it only provides a format to associate a summary with a template name. Mesh operators are encouraged to migrate to registered template types, which enable multiple-language interfaces and allow the mesh to derive proper matching semantics for attribute values. Methods like Netscape's RDM and the STARTS project allow unregistered template types to be understood through peer-to-peer agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: Some index cards follow a standard format (like library cards), and some are homemade. Standard formats are easier to understand, but people can agree on homemade ones too.

sections.title: Matching and Interoperability
sections.content: When a query searches for an attribute value, the match should be case-insensitive on the attribute name (so author, Author and AUTHOR all match Author-1). The matching semantics for the actual value depend on its data type and encoding. For registered template types, this information is known. For unregistered types, the default is octet-by-octet comparison, though mesh operators may apply case-insensitive substring matching for known text attributes. Over time, mesh maintainers can define restricted template types containing only attributes known to produce correct referrals, improving query effectiveness.
sections.plainLanguage: When looking for an author, the system doesn't care about uppercase or lowercase. For well-defined attribute types, the system knows whether to look for exact matches or partial ones.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
SOIF contains no requirement that template types include authentication attributes, so summary objects without authentication cannot be trusted. A hostile actor could create summaries that badly misrepresent a resource's content. If such a poisoned summary is included in the mesh, it could channel requests to the wrong server (denial of service) or away from a legitimate server (loss of visibility).

Because these summaries guide search queries, integrity of the mesh depends on the trustworthiness of the servers that create and share them.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone writes a fake catalog card about a book, other libraries might not know it is wrong. They might send people to the wrong place or away from the right place.
